name: Hungary water

lead: Hungary water is a rosemary-based distillate in brandy or alcohol, regarded as one of Europe's first alcohol-based perfumes. Legend ties it to a Hungarian queen, and it was used as a scent, a remedy and a beauty water.
For appearance, historical recipes recommended washing the face with it, often diluted in other distilled waters, and it was believed to help preserve a youthful look. No modern trials exist.

paras: Historically it was applied to the skin or face, mixed into other waters for washing, or sipped as a tonic; recipes varied over time.
No modern safety studies exist. Alcohol-based herbal preparations can irritate skin, and historical recipes varied.

chain: Rosemary-alcohol water applied or mixed into face washes
Believed to keep skin clear and fresh
angle.text: Users applied it to the face as a toner or wash, believing it kept skin clear and preserved youthfulness. This is a historical claim, not a tested result.

lead: Hungary water, also called the Queen of Hungary's water, was one of Europe's earliest alcohol-based perfumes, made mainly from rosemary [1][2]. Its origin is uncertain; some sources give around 1370 and credit Queen Elisabeth of Hungary, while other legends name a hermit, alchemist or monk, and many of these stories date from the 1600s [1].

As a beauty product, recipes advised washing with it, and it was often added to other distilled waters used on the face, with the belief that it prevented irritation and breakouts and helped preserve a youthful appearance [1]. Grokipedia likewise describes it as applied to tone the skin and preserve beauty, and taken as a remedy [2].

The oldest recipes distilled rosemary and thyme in brandy; later versions added ingredients such as lavender, mint, sage, marjoram, orange blossom and lemon [1]. It was eventually supplanted by Eau de Cologne in the 1700s [1].

paras: Legends place it in the 1370s at the court of Queen Elisabeth, said to have used it for headaches or failing eyesight; other tales name a hermit or alchemist [1][2]. Reports of it spread to France, with Montpellier later known for high-quality versions and newspaper advertisements warning of counterfeits [1].
In the late 1600s it was treated as a cure-all taken or applied for headaches and toothaches and used by men, women and children [1].
Recipes advised washing the face with it or diluting it in other waters, and it was linked with preserving a youthful appearance [1].
